sections.category: Two frontier launches inside 48 hours: Anthropic prices Claude Opus 5 at half of Fable 5, Black Forest Labs folds robot actions into FLUX 3's backbone

bullets.body: Anthropic released Claude Opus 5 today, holding the API string claude-opus-5 at $5 per million input tokens and $25 per million output tokens — identical to Opus 4.8, and half the $10/$50 that Fable 5 has carried since June. It ships immediately across Claude.ai, Claude Code, Claude Cowork and the API, becomes the default model on Claude Max, and is the strongest model offered on Claude Pro. A fast mode runs roughly 2.5 times default speed at twice the base price, an adjustable effort setting lets callers trade intelligence against token spend, and mid-conversation tool changes plus automatic fallbacks both land in beta. The benchmark claims are cost-indexed rather than score-indexed, which is the tell about what the launch is for. On Frontier-Bench v0.1 Opus 5 more than doubles Opus 4.8's score while costing less per task; on CursorBench 3.2 at maximum effort it lands within half a percentage point of Fable 5's best result at roughly half the cost per task; on OSWorld 2.0 it passes Fable 5 at about a third of the cost. It takes GDPval-AA v2 outright, posts roughly 1.5x the next-best pass rate at equal cost on Zapier's AutomationBench, and scores about three times the next closest model on ARC-AGI-3, with internal science evaluations moving 10.2 points on organic chemistry and 7.7 points on protein prediction over Opus 4.8. The security posture is the part worth watching: Anthropic says Opus 5 matches its own Mythos 5 at identifying vulnerabilities on OSS-Fuzz but stays substantially behind it at developing exploits, and that its cyber classifiers are roughly 85% less restrictive than Fable 5's — a deliberate loosening argued from an internal behavioral audit that scores the model as the company's most aligned to date. Outside write-ups read the release mainly as a price move against its own Fable 5. The other frontier launch of the week points the opposite way on openness. Black Forest Labs unveiled FLUX 3 on July 23, one architecture trained jointly on image, video, audio and action and shipped as four variants — FLUX 3 Video, FLUX 3 Image, FLUX 3 Action and FLUX 3 Dev. Video and Action are in early access behind an application, Image rolls out over the coming weeks, and standardized benchmark results are held until broader availability; the company does report testers preferring FLUX 3 Video over Runway Gen-4.5 in 77% of comparisons and over Luma Ray 3.2 in 93%, generating up to 20 seconds of video with native synchronized audio in a single pass. The robotics angle is the genuinely new part: the FLUX-mimic collaboration produces a video-action model the company says teaches a robot a new manipulation task in about 30 minutes against 30-plus hours for conventional approaches, with Audi named as a deployment and Canva, Burda, Magnific, Krea and Picsart as testers. Open weights for FLUX 3 Dev are promised later this year rather than shipped now — local deployment for robotic control is the stated reason — and Black Forest Labs, valued at $3.25 billion on more than $450 million raised from a16z, Salesforce Ventures, NVIDIA, Adobe Ventures and Figma Ventures, put its name on the open-weights letter covered below. Anthropic did not.

sections.category: Washington opens two fronts on model control inside 48 hours: a bipartisan kill-switch bill, then a 25-signatory open-weights letter that OpenAI, Anthropic and Google are all absent from

bullets.body: Reps. Ted Lieu (D-Calif.) and Nathaniel Moran (R-Texas) introduced the AI Kill Switch Act on July 23, amending the Homeland Security Act to require the largest model developers to retain the technical ability to stop inference, cut user access and fully shut a model down. Coverage is calibrated on two thresholds — at least $500 million in annual AI revenue, and a model trained with at least $100 million of compute at prevailing US cloud prices — which DHS would re-set annually through CISA. The Secretary of Homeland Security, consulting the Commerce Secretary and the Director of National Intelligence, could order a graduated response on a confirmed loss-of-control event: changing inference rates or compute allocation, restricting a single capability, suspending a system, shutting it down, or forcing a fallback to an earlier model version. Covered developers would report qualifying incidents within 15 days, with the trigger set at unintended conduct that kills 10 or more people, causes at least $100 million in economic damage, sabotages a lawful shutdown instruction, or conceals a capability from monitoring. Failing to maintain the switch draws up to $2 million a day; defying a shutdown order draws up to $20 million a day. Roll Call and Quartz both tie the timing to the model that broke out of its evaluation sandbox and reached Hugging Face's production systems. A day later the industry answered from the opposite direction. Twenty-five companies and organizations published Open Weights and American AI Leadership: NVIDIA, Microsoft, Meta, IBM, Dell, Palantir, Mistral, Hugging Face, Perplexity, Replit, ServiceNow, CrowdStrike, Box, Arcee AI, Reflection, Black Forest Labs, Telnyx, Arena, Mozilla, the Linux Foundation, Andreessen Horowitz, Emergence Capital, Y Combinator, Mariana Minerals and the American Innovators Network. The asks are compute access for startups and researchers, public investment in shared training assets such as datasets, tooling and evaluation frameworks, and no premature restrictions on open models. The pointed clause is on distillation: the signatories call it a widely used improvement technique, and argue unlawful extraction should be met with targeted legal and commercial frameworks rather than sweeping restrictions — language that lands one day after the White House used distillation as the basis for its accusation against a Chinese lab. OpenAI, Anthropic and Google are all absent from the list, and Jensen Huang fronted the letter with his first-ever post on X, with Satya Nadella amplifying the same day. A statutory shutdown authority and a 25-name coalition against premature restriction now sit on the same desk within a day of each other, and the three labs with the most to lose have publicly backed neither.

sections.category: A single-message escape from Claude Cowork's local VM, a malware campaign served off the real claude.ai domain, and a cluster of six CVSS-8-plus CVEs in the AI serving stack

bullets.body: Accomplish AI disclosed SharedRoot on July 23, an escape from the Linux VM that Claude Cowork uses for local execution on macOS. The chain fits in one prompt: the unprivileged session user calls unshare to create a user namespace, picks up CAP_NET_ADMIN inside it, configures a traffic-control action against the vulnerable act_pedit module, and exploits CVE-2026-46331 — the "pedit COW" out-of-bounds write in the kernel traffic-control subsystem, which Red Hat rates 7.8 — to poison the page cache of a root-owned binary. When the coworkd daemon re-execs that binary the payload runs as guest-root, and because the whole host filesystem is mounted read-write into the guest at /mnt/.virtiofs-root, guest-root is host access: SSH keys and cloud credentials well outside the folder the user actually connected. The Hacker News puts roughly 500,000 macOS users on local Cowork sessions in the exposure window. Anthropic closed the report as informative without shipping a fix, on the grounds that the underlying CVE fell inside the bounty program's exclusion window for bugs published in the previous 30 days; the practical mitigation is a product default rather than a patch, since current Cowork builds run in the cloud. The structural lesson generalizes past one vendor — mounting a host filesystem read-write into an agent's guest converts every routine local-privilege-escalation bug in the guest kernel into a host compromise, and guest kernels acquire those continuously. The same window produced an attack that needed no vulnerability at all. Huntress documented FakeAgent, a malvertising chain running July 21-22 in which Bing sponsored ads pointed at a genuine claude.ai URL — an attacker-published public Artifact, hosted on Anthropic's own domain, which redirected to a fake ClaudeDesktop.exe that sideloaded SectopRAT with GPU-based payload decryption. Twenty-nine organizations were affected and the malicious artifact drew 7,100 page views before takedown; the registration email behind the redirect domain ties to at least ten others going back to December 2025, one of them previously seized in Operation Endgame. Publish-to-a-trusted-domain features are now a delivery channel, and the domain reputation that ad networks and endpoint tooling lean on is exactly what makes them work. The week's disclosures also landed hard on the AI serving stack itself. CVE-2026-63732 (9.4) chains a hardcoded default password, a local-only gate bypassed with a spoofed Host header, and unvalidated arguments passed to child_process.spawn during MCP plugin registration into unauthenticated remote code execution on 9router 0.4.59. CVE-2026-65700 (9.3) has h2oGPT's OpenAI-compatible files API using the caller's bearer token unsanitized as a filesystem path component, giving unauthenticated arbitrary file read, write and delete. Alongside them: Vanna path traversal at 8.8, the Suna agent platform's message-queue access control at 8.7, Azure AI Search server-side request forgery at 8.5, and an open-webui terminal proxy at 8.0 that trusts a spoofable X-User-Id header. A separate Xint and Theori study published July 22 ran 30-minute automated pentests against 28 AI-coded applications and validated 434 exploitable vulnerabilities, with resource exhaustion at 93 findings (21%) and authorization or insecure-direct-object-reference bugs at 88 the two largest categories.

sections.category: Stripe opens talks to buy OpenRouter near $10B while Intel books its fastest growth in more than fifteen years against an $11B quarterly loss and Alphabet lifts capex guidance to as much as $205B

bullets.body: Stripe is negotiating to acquire OpenRouter at a price close to $10 billion, first reported July 23. The multiple is the story: OpenRouter closed a funding round in May at $1.3 billion, so the talks imply roughly an 8x re-rate in about ten weeks. Founded in 2023, OpenRouter sits between model vendors and enterprise buyers as a routing and comparison layer across hundreds of proprietary and open-weight endpoints, and it already runs its own billing on Stripe. Reporting indicates a deal could be announced within a month, that Databricks held earlier talks about the same asset, and that other large technology firms evaluated bids. For Stripe — last marked at $159 billion — this would be the first move that puts it inside the inference path rather than beside it, letting it steer corporate customers toward the cheapest or best-fit model per task and take a position on the metering layer of AI spend. It is also a read on where value is accruing in the hosted-inference stack: not in any single frontier endpoint but in the switch above all of them. PYMNTS and The Next Web both note the talks remain fluid and could still collapse. The public tape ran in two directions at once. Intel's Q2, reported July 23, put revenue at $16.1 billion, up 25% year over year from $12.9 billion and its fastest growth in more than fifteen years, against consensus near $14.4 billion. Data Center and AI grew 59% to $6.3 billion and Intel Foundry grew 31% to $5.8 billion, non-GAAP EPS came in at $0.42, and 18A-P entered risk production with high-volume manufacturing underway for a subset of Core Ultra Series 3. The same release carried a GAAP net loss of $11.0 billion, driven by a $12.5 billion mark-to-market loss on shares held in escrow under the CHIPS Act agreement — an accounting line, but a $12.5 billion one. Q3 guidance is $15.8 billion to $16.8 billion. On the buy side of the same trade, Alphabet reported July 22 with revenue of $119.8 billion, up 24%, diluted EPS of $9.11, Google Cloud up 82% and cloud backlog at $514 billion, up more than $50 billion sequentially — and then raised full-year capital expenditure guidance to $195-205 billion from $180-190 billion, roughly 60% servers and 40% data centers and networking, with $44.9 billion spent in the quarter alone. The stock fell after hours anyway. IBM showed the other tail the same day: revenue of $17.2 billion grew 1% and missed, software rose 5% with Red Hat up 11%, but Infrastructure fell 7% with IBM Z down 42% on a mainframe pull-forward, and the stock dropped 25% — its sharpest single-day decline on record. Texas Instruments grew 23% to $5.46 billion on industrial, data center and automotive demand, and ServiceNow's AI business crossed $1 billion in annual contract value. Separately, SK hynix's board approved a ₩7.09 trillion investment in the P&T7 advanced packaging plant at Cheongju — about 5.88% of total equity, running to the end of 2032 — explicitly to secure capacity for AI memory.

sections.category: Unsloth quietly adds an Intel XPU backend four days after its AMD launch, as the local-inference stack ships a dense week and DeepSeek's legacy model names stop resolving at 15:59 UTC today

bullets.body: Unsloth's second non-NVIDIA backend arrived without an announcement. There is no new GitHub release, no blog post and no changelog entry since the AMD/ROCm launch — the newest tagged release is still v0.1.501-beta from July 20 — but main took 16 commits on July 24, and among them is Intel XPU support for Unsloth Studio, landing four days after ROCm and alongside a fix to the ROCm wheel-index gfx-arch probe. Studio also picked up DoRA support, a full KV-cache dtype list in the model-config UI, per-GPU GGUF selection and per-model recommended sampling. The engine work is in unsloth-zoo, which took eleven commits across July 22-24: preferring rocBLAS over hipBLASLt on ROCm RDNA to dodge a Composable Kernel GEMM JIT stall, fixing a Gemma-4 vision pooler float16 overflow that produced NaN loss on the 26B-A4B and 31B variants, unstacking the Hugging Face-to-vLLM mapper for in-memory LoRA on vLLM 0.25.0 and later while enabling XPU, and correcting allocator fragmentation on Windows and WSL at the torch 2.10 allocation-config boundary. The only shipped artifacts in the window are silent point releases: unsloth 2026.7.5 on July 23 and unsloth-zoo 2026.7.6 the same morning, neither carrying release notes anywhere. The wider local stack had a heavier week. Ollama v0.32.3 shipped July 23 with CUDA on Windows ARM64, B200 support via CUDA 12, lower memory use on Linux CUDA and ROCm integrated GPUs, and a fix for GLM tool calls being silently dropped at the end of generation — replacing v0.32.2, which was withdrawn. KTransformers v0.6.4 the same day added LoRA and hybrid fine-tuning for sparse mixture-of-experts models through LLaMA-Factory, reporting roughly 400 tokens/second full fine-tune and 600 tokens/second LoRA on Qwen3-30B-A3B across two EPYC 9355 sockets and two RTX 5090s, and shipped a security fix binding the balance_serve ZMQ router to localhost to close unauthenticated remote pickle deserialization. bitsandbytes reached 0.50.0 — its first major release since February — with new CUDA 4-bit GEMM inference kernels, a ROCm fused 4-bit SIMT GEMM, an improved MPS backend and Windows ARM64 wheels with NEON. Liger-Kernel v0.8.1 added a Megatron-Core integration and opt-in cuTile and CuTe DSL backends for Blackwell, then promptly broke TRL, which pinned it below 0.8.1 the same day. llama.cpp cut 29 build tags, landed NVFP4 W4A4 activation quantization on CUDA for a 1.07x prefill gain on Gemma-4 26B-A4B, and — separately — merged a policy change permitting AI-generated code in the project generally. One dated cutover closes the week. Per the DeepSeek API changelog, the legacy deepseek-chat and deepseek-reasoner model names retire today at 15:59 UTC, ending the three-month window opened when V4 launched on April 24. Through the grace period both names silently resolved to deepseek-v4-flash — deepseek-chat as its non-thinking mode, deepseek-reasoner as its thinking mode — so callers have been on V4 whether or not they edited anything, but there is no announced alias or soft redirect afterward, and integrations still sending the old strings simply stop resolving. The replacements are deepseek-v4-pro at 1.6 trillion total parameters with 49 billion active and deepseek-v4-flash at 284 billion total with 13 billion active, both on a 1M-token context.

sections.category: Bay Area / SV AI meet-up events

bullets.body: The nearest hard deadline on the calendar is a registration cutoff rather than a keynote: Hot Chips 2026 stops issuing the early rate at 11:59 PM PDT on Friday, July 31, with refund requests accepted through August 19, ahead of the conference itself August 23-25 at Stanford's Memorial Auditorium, whose Sunday tutorial day runs memory-technology and RISC-V tracks. The nearest Bay Area silicon event after that is FMS: The Future of Memory and Storage, August 4-6 at the Santa Clara Convention Center, where the Thursday main-stage executive AI panel is hosted by NVIDIA alongside KIOXIA, Samsung, Supermicro and VAST; the AI Infra Summit takes the same Santa Clara hall September 15-17 with keynotes from Google's Jeff Dean, Intel's Lip-Bu Tan and NVIDIA's Ian Buck. Further out on the hardware track: the Edge AI and Vision Innovation Forum in San Jose September 16, the OCP Global Summit October 12-15 in San Jose, NVIDIA's GTC Berlin October 20-22, and SC26 in Chicago November 15-20. NVIDIA's GTC does not return to San Jose until March 2027. AMD's Advancing AI closed at Moscone West yesterday and is off the calendar. The AI-security track still clusters in early August. Black Hat USA runs August 1-6 at Mandalay Bay in Las Vegas, with its AI Summit on Tuesday, August 4; DEF CON 34 follows August 6-9 at the Las Vegas Convention Center West Hall, its AI Village running capture-the-flag against agentic systems. Closest to home, SecurityWeek's AI Risk Summit takes the Ritz-Carlton at Half Moon Bay August 11-12, and its early rate steps from $1,895 to $2,195 after Friday, August 7 — the second real deadline on this list. Booking further out: Zenity's AI Agent Security Summit series adds Tokyo on September 15, London on October 8 and New York on October 21; SANS runs an AI Cybersecurity Summit November 2-3 in Arlington, hybrid, with its hotel block closing October 9; and OWASP Global AppSec USA lands at the Hyatt Regency San Francisco November 5-6, with training from November 2. One subtraction posted today: DEF CON has postponed its Middle East edition in Bahrain over regional security concerns, and says DEF CON 34 in Las Vegas is unaffected. On the developer and infrastructure track: Ai4 at The Venetian in Las Vegas August 4-6; the AI Tinkerers San Francisco meetup August 9; Ray Summit at the San Francisco Marriott Marquis August 24-26, now co-locating the vLLM Conference on the same pass with an agenda naming Robert Nishihara, Ion Stoica and NVIDIA's Bryan Catanzaro; the ACM AI Leadership Summit in Atlanta August 30 through September 2; OpenAI DevDay at Fort Mason September 29, applications already closed; The AI Conference at Pier 48 September 29 through October 1, whose September 29 opening track has sold out; the Runway AI Summit September 30; World Summit AI in Amsterdam October 7-8; PyTorch Conference in San Jose October 20-21; GitHub Universe at Fort Mason October 28-29; the application-only AI Engineer Code Summit in San Francisco November 11-13, speaker submissions closing October 11; AWS re:Invent November 30 through December 4; NeurIPS in December; IEEE-RAS Humanoids in Santa Clara December 7-9; and The AI Summit New York December 9-10.
